content.intro: Living organisms are made of cells. A cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life.

sections.heading: What is a cell?
sections.text: Cells are the smallest units that can carry out the processes necessary for life. Some organisms consist of one cell, while others consist of many cells.

sections.heading: Animal and plant cells
sections.text: Both plant and animal cells have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus. Plant cells also typically have a cell wall, a large permanent vacuole and chloroplasts in photosynthetic cells.

sections.heading: Functions of cell structures
sections.text: The nucleus contains genetic material and helps control cell activities. The cell membrane regulates the movement of substances into and out of the cell. Mitochondria release energy through cellular respiration.

content.example: A leaf cell may contain chloroplasts that absorb light energy for photosynthesis.
content.summary: Cells are the basic units of life. Cell structures have specialised functions, and plant cells have some structures that animal cells do not.

xh.title: Intshayelelo kwiiSeli
xh.intro: Izinto eziphilayo zenziwe ziiseli. Iseli yeyona yunithi isisiseko yokwakheka nokusebenza kobomi.
xh.summary: Iiseli zezona yunithi zisisiseko zobomi. Amalungu eseli anemisebenzi eyahlukeneyo.

quiz.question: What is the basic structural and functional unit of life?
quiz.explanation: A cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life.

quiz.question: Which structure is typically found in plant cells but not animal cells?
quiz.explanation: Plant cells have a cell wall outside the cell membrane. Animal cells do not have a cell wall.

quiz.question: Which organelle releases energy through cellular respiration?
quiz.explanation: Mitochondria are the main sites of aerobic cellular respiration.

content.intro: Photosynthesis is the process through which plants use light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water.

sections.heading: Where does photosynthesis happen?
sections.text: Photosynthesis takes place in chloroplasts. Chlorophyll, a green pigment, absorbs light energy.

sections.heading: What does a plant need?
sections.text: The main requirements are light energy, water and carbon dioxide. Water is absorbed by roots, while carbon dioxide enters leaves through small openings called stomata.

sections.heading: The photosynthesis equation
sections.text: Carbon dioxide and water are used to produce glucose and oxygen when light energy is available. The balanced equation is 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2, in the presence of light and chlorophyll.

content.example: A plant kept in darkness for a long period cannot sustain normal photosynthesis because it lacks the light energy needed for the process.
content.summary: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose. Oxygen is released as a by-product.

xh.title: Ifotosinthesisi
xh.intro: Ifotosinthesisi yinkqubo apho izityalo zisebenzisa amandla okukhanya ukwenza iswekile ngekharbon dayoksayidi namanzi.
xh.summary: Ifotosinthesisi iguqula amandla okukhanya abe ngamandla ekhemikhali agcinwe kwiswekile. Ioksijini iyakhutshwa.

quiz.question: In which organelle does photosynthesis take place?
quiz.explanation: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.

quiz.question: Which gas is released during photosynthesis?
quiz.explanation: Oxygen is released when water molecules are split during the light-dependent reactions.

quiz.question: Which substance stores chemical energy produced by photosynthesis?
quiz.explanation: Glucose stores chemical energy that plants can use in cellular respiration and other processes.

content.intro: Genetics is the study of inheritance and variation. DNA contains genetic instructions that influence the characteristics of organisms.

sections.heading: What is DNA?
sections.text: DNA stands for deoxyribonucleic acid. It carries genetic information and is organised into chromosomes in the nucleus of most human cells.

sections.heading: Genes and alleles
sections.text: A gene is a section of DNA associated with a particular functional product or characteristic. Different forms of the same gene are called alleles.

sections.heading: Genotype and phenotype
sections.text: Genotype refers to an organism's genetic makeup for a characteristic. Phenotype refers to the observable characteristics that result from genetic and environmental influences.

content.example: In a simple Mendelian example, if B represents a dominant allele and b a recessive allele, an individual with genotype Bb shows the dominant phenotype, assuming complete dominance.
content.summary: DNA carries genetic information. Genes have different alleles, and inherited genetic combinations contribute to an organism's phenotype.

xh.title: I-DNA noLifa
xh.intro: I-Genetics sisifundo selifa nokwahluka. I-DNA iqulethe imiyalelo yemfuza echaphazela iimpawu zezinto eziphilayo.
xh.summary: I-DNA ithwala ulwazi lwemfuza. Iijini zineendlela ezahlukeneyo ezibizwa ngokuba zii-alleles, nezinegalelo kwiimpawu zezinto eziphilayo.

quiz.question: What is an allele?
options: A different form of a gene
quiz.explanation: Alleles are different forms of the same gene.

quiz.question: What does phenotype mean?
options: The observable characteristics of an organism
quiz.explanation: Phenotype refers to observable characteristics shaped by genetic and environmental influences.
